Global CO₂ Emissions: Does GDP Predict Emissions and Does Carbon Tax Help?

Isuri

2026-04-07

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)
library(broom)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

1. Introduction

This case study investigates two related research questions about global CO₂ emissions:

Q1: Does GDP per capita predict CO₂ emissions per capita across countries?

Q2: Does having a carbon tax affect CO₂ emissions in top emitting countries?

Understanding the relationship between economic development, carbon pricing policy, and emissions is critical for designing effective climate policy. A naive analysis might suggest carbon tax increases emissions: this study demonstrates why controlling for confounding variables matters.

1.1 Data Sources

Dataset Source Coverage
CO₂ & Greenhouse Gas Emissions Our World in Data 164 countries, 2000–2024
Carbon Pricing Instrument Coverage World Bank 164 countries, 1989–2024

2. Data Loading & Cleaning

2.1 Load raw data

co2EmissionData <- read_csv("data/raw/co2-emission.csv",
                             show_col_types = FALSE)
carbonTaxData   <- read_csv("data/raw/carbon-tax-data.csv",
                             show_col_types = FALSE)

cat("CO2 dataset:", nrow(co2EmissionData), "rows x",
    ncol(co2EmissionData), "columns\n")
## CO2 dataset: 50411 rows x 79 columns
cat("Carbon tax dataset:", nrow(carbonTaxData), "rows x",
    ncol(carbonTaxData), "columns\n")
## Carbon tax dataset: 7236 rows x 4 columns

2.2 Clean carbon tax data

carbonTaxData <- carbonTaxData %>%
  rename(
    country        = Entity,
    iso_code       = Code,
    year           = Year,
    has_carbon_tax = `Covered by tax instrument in at least one sector`
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    carbon_tax = ifelse(has_carbon_tax == "No carbon tax",
                        FALSE, TRUE)
  ) %>%
  select(country, iso_code, year, carbon_tax) %>%
  filter(year >= 2000 & year <= 2024)

cat("Unique carbon_tax values:",
    paste(unique(carbonTaxData$carbon_tax), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Unique carbon_tax values: FALSE, TRUE

2.3 Clean CO₂ data

co2EmissionData <- co2EmissionData %>%
  filter(!is.na(iso_code),
         year >= 2000 & year <= 2024)

co2EmissionDataCleaned <- co2EmissionData %>%
  select(country, iso_code, year,
         gdp, population, co2,
         co2_per_capita, share_global_co2,
         primary_energy_consumption)

co2EmissionDataCleaned <- co2EmissionDataCleaned %>%
  arrange(country, year) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  mutate(
    gdp = ifelse(is.na(gdp),
                 mean(gdp, na.rm = TRUE), gdp),
    primary_energy_consumption = ifelse(
      is.na(primary_energy_consumption),
      mean(primary_energy_consumption, na.rm = TRUE),
      primary_energy_consumption)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

no_gdp_countries <- co2EmissionDataCleaned %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(all_na = all(is.na(gdp)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(all_na) %>%
  pull(country)

cat("Countries removed (no GDP data):",
    length(no_gdp_countries), "\n")
## Countries removed (no GDP data): 54
co2EmissionDataCleaned <- co2EmissionDataCleaned %>%
  filter(!country %in% no_gdp_countries) %>%
  mutate(gdp_per_capita = gdp / population)

cat("\nMissing values after cleaning:\n")
## 
## Missing values after cleaning:
print(colSums(is.na(co2EmissionDataCleaned)))
##                    country                   iso_code 
##                          0                          0 
##                       year                        gdp 
##                          0                          0 
##                 population                        co2 
##                          0                          0 
##             co2_per_capita           share_global_co2 
##                          0                          0 
## primary_energy_consumption             gdp_per_capita 
##                          0                          0

2.4 Join datasets

co2_tax_gdp <- co2EmissionDataCleaned %>%
  inner_join(
    carbonTaxData %>% select(iso_code, year, carbon_tax),
    by = c("iso_code", "year")
  )

cat("Final dataset:", nrow(co2_tax_gdp), "rows\n")
## Final dataset: 4100 rows
cat("Countries:", n_distinct(co2_tax_gdp$country), "\n")
## Countries: 164
cat("Year range:",
    paste(range(co2_tax_gdp$year), collapse = " to "), "\n")
## Year range: 2000 to 2024

3. Data Aggregation

country_avg <- co2_tax_gdp %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_co2_per_capita = mean(co2_per_capita,  na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_gdp_per_capita = mean(gdp_per_capita,  na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_share_global   = mean(share_global_co2, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_energy         = mean(primary_energy_consumption,
                              na.rm = TRUE),
    has_carbon_tax     = as.logical(max(carbon_tax,
                                        na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    gdp_level = case_when(
      avg_gdp_per_capita > 12000 ~ "High income",
      avg_gdp_per_capita > 3000  ~ "Middle income",
      TRUE                       ~ "Low income"
    ),
    gdp_level = factor(gdp_level,
                       levels = c("Low income",
                                  "Middle income",
                                  "High income"))
  )

top_countries <- co2_tax_gdp %>%
  filter(year >= 2018 & year <= 2024) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(avg_share = mean(share_global_co2, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_share)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  pull(country)

cat("Dataset dimensions:", nrow(country_avg),
    "countries\n")
## Dataset dimensions: 164 countries
cat("Top 20 emitters identified\n")
## Top 20 emitters identified

4. Exploratory Data Analysis

4.1 Distribution of CO₂ per capita

ggplot(country_avg, aes(x = avg_co2_per_capita)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#47B9C6",
                 color = "white") +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of Average CO2 Emissions per Capita",
    subtitle = "Right-skewed: most countries emit under 5 tonnes",
    x = "Average CO2 per Capita (tonnes)",
    y = "Number of Countries"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

The distribution is strongly right-skewed. Most countries emit fewer than 5 tonnes per capita, while a small number of high-income and fossil-fuel-dependent nations are significant outliers above 15 tonnes.

4.2 Top 20 countries by global CO₂ share

country_avg %>%
  filter(country %in% top_countries) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_share_global)) %>%
  mutate(top5 = row_number() <= 5) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, avg_share_global),
             y = avg_share_global, fill = top5)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#21497E", "FALSE" = "#ACE9DF"),
    guide  = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Top 20 Countries by Average Share of Global CO2",
    subtitle = "China and USA account for ~42% of global emissions",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Average Share of Global CO2 (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

China (25%) and the United States (17%) dominate global emissions. The top 5 emitters together account for over 55% of global CO₂.

4.3 Carbon tax adoption

carbon_tax_dist <- country_avg %>%
  group_by(has_carbon_tax) %>%
  summarise(count = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    pct   = round(count / sum(count) * 100, 1),
    label = ifelse(has_carbon_tax,
                   "Has Carbon Tax", "No Carbon Tax")
  )

ggplot(carbon_tax_dist,
       aes(x = 2, y = pct, fill = label)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1,
           color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  xlim(0.5, 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(label, "\n", pct, "%")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Has Carbon Tax" = "#47B9C6",
    "No Carbon Tax"  = "#ACE9DF"
  )) +
  labs(title = "Carbon Tax Adoption Across Countries") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5,
                                  face = "bold",
                                  size = 14))

Only 17.1% of countries have adopted a carbon tax. This limited adoption makes cross-country comparison feasible but means the taxed group is a minority.

4.4 GDP per capita vs CO₂ per capita

country_avg %>%
  filter(country %in% top_countries) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_gdp_per_capita,
             y = avg_co2_per_capita)) +
  geom_point(color = "#47B9C6", size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              color = "#21497E", fill = "#ACE9DF",
              alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = country),
                  size = 3, color = "grey30") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format()) +
  labs(
    title    = "GDP per Capita vs CO2 per Capita (Top 20 Emitters)",
    subtitle = "Strong positive linear relationship",
    x = "Average GDP per Capita (USD)",
    y = "Average CO2 per Capita (tonnes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

A clear positive relationship is visible. Notable exceptions include Saudi Arabia (high emissions relative to GDP) and Germany/UK (lower emissions than GDP would predict, possibly due to carbon pricing and energy efficiency policies).

4.5 CO₂ per capita by country coloured by carbon tax

country_avg %>%
  filter(country %in% top_countries) %>%
  arrange(avg_co2_per_capita) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, avg_co2_per_capita),
             y = avg_co2_per_capita,
             fill = has_carbon_tax)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TRUE"  = "#47B9C6",
               "FALSE" = "#ACE9DF"),
    labels = c("TRUE"  = "Has Carbon Tax",
               "FALSE" = "No Carbon Tax"),
    name   = "Carbon Tax"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Average CO2 per Capita: Top 20 Emitters",
    subtitle = "Carbon tax countries not consistently lower emitters",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Average CO2 per Capita (tonnes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Countries with carbon tax are not consistently lower emitters: Australia and Canada have high emissions despite carbon tax. This confirms GDP confounding motivates the regression analysis below.

4.6 GDP vs CO₂ coloured by carbon tax

country_avg %>%
  filter(country %in% top_countries) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_gdp_per_capita,
             y = avg_co2_per_capita,
             color = has_carbon_tax)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = country),
                  size = 2.8) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE"  = "#47B9C6",
               "FALSE" = "gray50"),
    labels = c("TRUE"  = "Has Carbon Tax",
               "FALSE" = "No Carbon Tax"),
    name   = "Carbon Tax"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format()) +
  labs(
    title    = "GDP vs CO2 per Capita: Coloured by Carbon Tax",
    subtitle = "High-GDP carbon tax countries cluster above the trend line",
    x = "Average GDP per Capita (USD)",
    y = "Average CO2 per Capita (tonnes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

High-GDP countries with carbon tax (Germany, UK, Japan) sit below where the trend line would place them: suggesting carbon tax may be contributing to lower-than-expected emissions at high income levels.

5. Correlation Analysis

5.1 Q1 : GDP per capita vs CO₂ per capita

cor_q1 <- cor.test(
  country_avg$avg_gdp_per_capita,
  country_avg$avg_co2_per_capita,
  method = "pearson"
)

tidy(cor_q1) %>%
  select(estimate, statistic, p.value,
         conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 4))) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Pearson Correlation: GDP vs CO2 per Capita",
    col.names = c("r", "t-statistic", "p-value",
                  "CI lower", "CI upper")
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
Pearson Correlation: GDP vs CO2 per Capita
r t-statistic p-value CI lower CI upper
0.8236 18.4812 0 0.7672 0.8674

There is a strong positive correlation between GDP per capita and CO₂ per capita (r = 0.824, p < 0.001). The 95% confidence interval confirms this is a reliable and substantial relationship. Wealthier countries consistently emit more CO₂ per person.

5.2 Q2 : Carbon tax vs CO₂ per capita

cor_q2 <- cor.test(
  as.numeric(country_avg$has_carbon_tax),
  country_avg$avg_co2_per_capita,
  method = "pearson"
)

tidy(cor_q2) %>%
  select(estimate, statistic, p.value,
         conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 4))) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Pearson Correlation: Carbon Tax vs CO2 per Capita",
    col.names = c("r", "t-statistic", "p-value",
                  "CI lower", "CI upper")
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
Pearson Correlation: Carbon Tax vs CO2 per Capita
r t-statistic p-value CI lower CI upper
0.2136 2.7836 0.006 0.0624 0.3553

Without controlling for GDP, carbon tax shows a weak positive correlation with CO₂ per capita (r = 0.214, p = 0.006). This counterintuitive direction is explained by GDP confounding : richer countries both adopt carbon tax and emit more per capita. This motivates the controlled regression analysis below.

5.3 Correlation summary

data.frame(
  Relationship        = c("GDP per capita → CO2 per capita",
                          "Carbon tax → CO2 per capita"),
  r                   = c(round(cor_q1$estimate, 3),
                          round(cor_q2$estimate, 3)),
  p_value             = c(round(cor_q1$p.value, 6),
                          round(cor_q2$p.value, 4)),
  Interpretation      = c("Strong positive : significant",
                          "Weak positive : confounded by GDP")
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Correlation Analysis Summary") %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
Correlation Analysis Summary
Relationship r p_value Interpretation
GDP per capita → CO2 per capita 0.824 0.000 Strong positive : significant
Carbon tax → CO2 per capita 0.214 0.006 Weak positive : confounded by GDP

6. Regression Analysis

6.1 Model 1 : GDP alone

m1 <- lm(avg_co2_per_capita ~ avg_gdp_per_capita,
         data = country_avg)

tidy(m1) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 5))) %>%
  kable(caption = "Model 1: GDP per Capita → CO2 per Capita") %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
Model 1: GDP per Capita → CO2 per Capita
term estimate std.error statistic p.value
(Intercept) -0.00012 0.38604 -0.00032 0.99974
avg_gdp_per_capita 0.00030 0.00002 18.48122 0.00000 
glance(m1) %>%
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared,
         sigma, p.value, nobs) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 4))) %>%
  kable(caption = "Model 1 : Model Performance") %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
Model 1 : Model Performance
r.squared adj.r.squared sigma p.value nobs
0.6783 0.6763 3.6113 0 164

GDP per capita alone explains 67.8% of variation in CO₂ per capita. For every $10,000 increase in GDP per capita, CO₂ per capita increases by approximately 3.02 tonnes.

6.2 Model 2 : Carbon tax alone

m2 <- lm(avg_co2_per_capita ~ has_carbon_tax,
         data = country_avg)

tidy(m2) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 4))) %>%
  kable(caption = "Model 2: Carbon Tax → CO2 per Capita") %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
Model 2: Carbon Tax → CO2 per Capita
term estimate std.error statistic p.value
(Intercept) 4.2588 0.5334 7.9850 0.000
has_carbon_taxTRUE 3.5931 1.2908 2.7836 0.006

Without controlling for GDP, having a carbon tax is associated with +3.59 tonnes more CO₂ per capita. This is misleading : it reflects that wealthy countries adopt carbon tax AND emit more due to their economic scale.

6.3 Model 3 : GDP + Carbon tax

m3 <- lm(avg_co2_per_capita ~ avg_gdp_per_capita + has_carbon_tax,
         data = country_avg)

tidy(m3) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 5))) %>%
  kable(caption = "Model 3: GDP + Carbon Tax → CO2 per Capita") %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
Model 3: GDP + Carbon Tax → CO2 per Capita
term estimate std.error statistic p.value
(Intercept) 0.04384 0.36906 0.11878 0.90560
avg_gdp_per_capita 0.00033 0.00002 19.11234 0.00000
has_carbon_taxTRUE -3.24271 0.80050 -4.05084 0.00008 
glance(m3) %>%
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared,
         sigma, p.value, nobs) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 4))) %>%
  kable(caption = "Model 3 : Model Performance") %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
Model 3 : Model Performance
r.squared adj.r.squared sigma p.value nobs
0.708 0.7044 3.4509 0 164

After controlling for GDP, carbon tax is associated with -3.24 tonnes less CO₂ per capita (p < 0.001). The sign completely flips from positive to negative : confirming GDP as a confounding variable. Together GDP and carbon tax explain 70.8% of CO₂ variation.

6.4 Model comparison

data.frame(
  Model = c(
    "M1: GDP alone",
    "M2: Carbon tax alone",
    "M3: GDP + Carbon tax"
  ),
  R_squared = c(
    round(glance(m1)$r.squared, 3),
    round(glance(m2)$r.squared, 3),
    round(glance(m3)$r.squared, 3)
  ),
  Carbon_tax_coef = c(
    "N/A",
    paste0("+", round(tidy(m2)$estimate[2], 3)),
    round(tidy(m3)$estimate[3], 3)
  ),
  Interpretation = c(
    "GDP explains 67.8% alone",
    "Misleading positive : GDP confounded",
    "True effect after GDP control"
  )
) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Model Comparison : Carbon Tax Coefficient",
    col.names = c("Model", "R²",
                  "Carbon tax coefficient",
                  "Interpretation")
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  ) %>%
  row_spec(3, bold = TRUE, background = "#ACE9DF")
Model Comparison : Carbon Tax Coefficient
Model R² Carbon tax coefficient Interpretation
M1: GDP alone 0.678 N/A GDP explains 67.8% alone
M2: Carbon tax alone 0.046 +3.593 Misleading positive : GDP confounded
M3: GDP + Carbon tax 0.708 -3.243 True effect after GDP control

6.5 Actual vs fitted plot

country_avg %>%
  mutate(fitted = fitted(m3)) %>%
  filter(country %in% top_countries) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fitted,
             y = avg_co2_per_capita,
             color = has_carbon_tax,
             label = country)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed",
              color = "#21497E") +
  geom_text_repel(size = 2.8) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE"  = "#47B9C6",
               "FALSE" = "gray50"),
    labels = c("TRUE"  = "Has Carbon Tax",
               "FALSE" = "No Carbon Tax"),
    name   = "Carbon Tax"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Actual vs Fitted CO2 per Capita (Model 3)",
    subtitle = "Points close to dashed line = well predicted by model",
    x = "Fitted values",
    y = "Actual CO2 per Capita (tonnes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Points close to the dashed line are well predicted by the model. Saudi Arabia sits well above : its emissions are higher than the model predicts given its GDP, suggesting fossil fuel dependence beyond what income alone explains.

7. Key Findings

data.frame(
  Finding = c(
    "GDP strongly predicts CO2",
    "Carbon tax misleading without control",
    "Carbon tax reduces CO2 after GDP control",
    "Model explanatory power",
    "Confounding variable confirmed"
  ),
  Detail = c(
    "r = 0.824, p < 0.001 : strong positive relationship",
    "Without GDP: +3.59 tonnes (positive, misleading)",
    "With GDP control: -3.24 tonnes (p < 0.001)",
    "GDP + tax explains 70.8% of CO2 variation (R2 = 0.708)",
    "GDP is a confounder : direction flips when controlled"
  )
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Summary of Key Findings") %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = TRUE
  ) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, color = "#21497E")
Summary of Key Findings
Finding Detail
GDP strongly predicts CO2 r = 0.824, p < 0.001 : strong positive relationship
Carbon tax misleading without control Without GDP: +3.59 tonnes (positive, misleading)
Carbon tax reduces CO2 after GDP control With GDP control: -3.24 tonnes (p < 0.001)
Model explanatory power GDP + tax explains 70.8% of CO2 variation (R2 = 0.708)
Confounding variable confirmed GDP is a confounder : direction flips when controlled

Q1 Answer

GDP per capita is a strong and statistically significant predictor of CO₂ emissions per capita (r = 0.824, R² = 0.678). For every $10,000 increase in GDP per capita, a country emits approximately 3.2 additional tonnes of CO₂ per person per year.

Q2 Answer

Carbon tax does reduce CO₂ emissions, but only after controlling for GDP. Without the control, it appears to increase emissions : a classic example of confounding. After accounting for GDP, carbon tax is associated with 3.24 fewer tonnes of CO₂ per capita (p < 0.001).

8. Limitations

data.frame(
  Limitation = c(
    "Small sample",
    "Binary tax variable",
    "Cross-sectional aggregation",
    "Omitted variables",
    "Causality"
  ),
  Detail = c(
    "Only 164 countries: limits statistical power",
    "Carbon tax is yes/no: does not capture tax rate or coverage",
    "Country averages mask year-to-year variation",
    "Energy mix, industrial structure, and policy stringency not included",
    "Regression shows association, not causation"
  )
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Study Limitations") %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = TRUE
  )
Study Limitations
Limitation Detail
Small sample Only 164 countries: limits statistical power
Binary tax variable Carbon tax is yes/no: does not capture tax rate or coverage
Cross-sectional aggregation Country averages mask year-to-year variation
Omitted variables Energy mix, industrial structure, and policy stringency not included
Causality Regression shows association, not causation
